summary:
Penumbra is a survival planner for lunar south-pole landers, built for the "Lunar Landing Site Navigator" challenge in "The Next Frontier". Near the pole the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees above the horizon, so "the interaction of grazing sunlight and large local topography variations leads to extreme illumination conditions" (Gläser et al. 2018, doi 10.1016/j.pss.2017.07.006). The challenge says "Small changes in landing location or date can dramatically affect both power generation potential and communication windows." In our own model output, landing at IM-2's site 2 days early (2026-11-12 instead of 2026-11-14) takes operable time from 15.9 days to 0 h. IM-1 and IM-2 both landed near the pole and ended early.

For any site and landing date, Penumbra tells a planner how many hours of sunlight and Earth contact the lander gets, and when the first shadow arrives that would drain its battery. It builds a 360° terrain horizon from NASA LOLA elevation maps and computes Sun and Earth positions from JPL's DE440 ephemeris. A battery model then turns those into an operable window and a time to first lethal shadow.

One Rust model runs natively for validation and in the browser as WebAssembly. A public scoreboard checks it against outside judges: JPL Horizons (V1, pass), NASA's LOLA illumination map (V2, pass), published longest-night figures (V2b, reported as a fail), the IM-2 reconstruction (V4), and red-team edge cases (V5, 7 of 7).
details:
What it does
Pick a south-pole site, a landing date and a mast height, or a curated site (IM-2, SP-01, Barker Site 1). Penumbra shows the operable hours (Sun and Earth contact at once), the time to the first lethal shadow, operable days for the next 30 landing dates, the slope at the pin from the 20 m DEM, a horizon panorama with the Sun and Earth tracks, timelines with uncertainty bands on each sunrise and sunset, a 3D terrain view, a side-by-side comparison of two sites or dates, and a replay of IM-2's landing site and date. A region heatmap over Mons Mouton shows the nearest spot that would have kept the lander running longer.

How it works
1. Horizon: ray-marching the NASA LOLA terrain with lunar curvature, in three tiers (20 m out to 7 km, 80 m to 31 km, 240 m beyond).
2. Sun and Earth: topocentric positions in the Moon's mean-Earth frame from the NAIF DE440 kernels, including light time and aberration.
3. Visibility: the fraction of the Sun's disc above the horizon, kept apart from "any part visible", the metric NASA's maps use.
4. Battery: a state-of-charge model for a lander preset finds when stored energy runs out.
5. Uncertainty: sunset and sunrise bands from the LOLA height-error map.

Validation
Every check runs against a source we did not build, and misses are reported, not tuned away. JPL Horizons: worst Sun or Earth angle difference 0.00011 degrees against a 0.002 degree threshold (V1, pass). NASA LOLA average-visibility map: pooled median error 0.48 points (V2, pass). Published longest-night figures (V2b): fails at SP-01 by 0.21 days, shown in the app. LROC NAC shadow comparison (V3): not run, because the images were not downloaded. IM-2 reconstruction (V4) and red-team edge cases (V5, 7 of 7).

Benefits and impact
Landing sites near the pole live or die by a few hundred metres or a couple of days. Penumbra gives planners, educators and the public those answers in a browser in seconds, free, with no account and no backend.

Tools and languages
Rust (core model, offline pipeline, WebAssembly via wasm-bindgen) with the ANISE crate for SPICE kernels; TypeScript with Svelte 5 and Vite, Three.js for 3D and uPlot for timelines; Bun and Playwright for scripts and tests; Typst for the project document; Cloudflare Pages for hosting.

Source code (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/qicai14/penumbra

Team Fractured Toes
Lim Qi Cai (team lead): idea and research, the science model and data pipeline, validation, CI and deploy, web app features, the project paper.
Charls Pua Vui Hau: web app UI and tests, design and wireframes, the poster and the videos.

30 second demo: https://youtu.be/7Xwj2baNhtI
5 minute pitch: https://youtu.be/pQfO0rvDjDo
